# What does OBDII fault code P0120 really mean?

When an engine control unit (ECU) logs fault code P0120, it is reporting a "Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor 'A' Circuit Malfunction." To a developer debugging firmware or analyzing telemetry, this isn't just a generic error; it indicates a disruption in the feedback loop between the driver's input and the engine management system. The source material highlights a specific vehicle, a Renault Kangoo, exhibiting symptoms like hard starting, uncontrolled acceleration, and intermittent "electric fault" warnings that clear upon restart. These are classic signs of an ECU receiving inconsistent or out-of-range voltage signals from either the Throttle-Body Position Sensor (TPS) or the Pedal Position Sensor (PPS).

The confusion often stems from the shared nomenclature in the code definition: "Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor." In modern drive-by-wire architectures, these are distinct components with separate circuit paths. The TPS resides under the bonnet on the throttle body, measuring the actual valve opening to regulate airflow. Conversely, the PPS is mounted on the accelerator pedal, translating foot pressure into a voltage signal that commands the throttle actuator. A malfunction in either component triggers P0120, but the underlying cause differs significantly in terms of debugging strategy and hardware replacement.

If the vehicle experiences uncontrolled acceleration, the system likely received a "floor it" signal from the PPS while the TPS reported a closed or partially open position. This creates a safety conflict where the ECU attempts to limit power based on throttle valve data but is forced to obey pedal demand data. In such scenarios, the ECU may enter a fail-safe mode, limiting engine power to prevent catastrophic failure. This explains why the car might be hard to start in the mornings; if the startup sequence fails to initialize the sensor calibration or if the voltage exceeds acceptable thresholds during cranking, the ECU may refuse to engage the fuel injection or ignition timing correctly until the fault clears.

Diagnosing which specific sensor is at fault requires isolating the circuit behavior rather than guessing. A logical approach involves measuring resistance and voltage across the signal wires with a multimeter while manually manipulating the pedal and throttle. If the PPS circuit shows an open loop (infinite resistance) or a short to ground, the issue lies in the wiring harness connecting the pedal to the ECU, which is common in Renault Kangoo models due to stress on the connector plug. If the voltage remains static at 0V or battery voltage regardless of input movement, the sensor module itself has likely failed internally.

It is also possible that both sensors are not simultaneously faulty, but rather that a shared power supply rail or ground reference point is compromised. Since these sensors often share a common ground within the engine bay, a corroded chassis ground can cause erratic readings on both circuits. Before replacing expensive sensors, verifying the integrity of the grounding points and checking for water ingress in the connector housings is a critical step. Ignoring corrosion issues leads to recurring faults that persist even after component replacement.

From a software perspective, if you are working with ECU logs, look for "limp mode" states or torque reduction flags associated with this code. The intermittent nature of the warning light suggests an unstable connection rather than a total short circuit. Developers should implement hysteresis in their diagnostic routines to avoid triggering permanent fault codes during transient voltage dips caused by electrical load spikes.

For those managing vehicle data platforms, integrating real-time sensor normalization can help distinguish between a hard sensor failure and a temporary signal noise event. The specific behavior of the Renault Kangoo suggests that mechanical linkage wear or connector fatigue on the pedal side is a more probable culprit than a complete electronic failure of both sensors. Addressing the root cause of the circuit malfunction requires precise electrical testing rather than blind part replacement.
